title: Gandhi's Gita
hook: the word Gandhi put on the cover: anasakti

segments.voice: Yesterday in Gandhi's Gita, the battlefield moved inside: Gandhi read the Gita's field as the human heart, and Krishna as the dweller within. Where did you notice two pulls in yourself? Your line was the battle is inside. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

A woman plants a row of mango saplings at the edge of a village. She may not be living there when the first fruit comes, and somebody else's children will climb those branches. She waters them anyway, every evening, carefully, as if the harvest were hers. Is that foolish, or is it the whole point? When Gandhi made his own Gita in Gujarati, he didn't name it after Krishna or after the battle. He named it after one idea, and that idea is the shape of what she's doing. Today, the word on the cover.
screen: `SHE PLANTS FOR A HARVEST SHE MAY NOT SEE.` → `SHE WATERS THEM ANYWAY.` → `THE WORD ON THE COVER.`

segments.voice: The title is Anasakti Yoga. Anasakti is usually put into English as non-attachment, or selfless action: doing the work without clinging to what it gets you. Gandhi said this was the Gita's central teaching, the one the rest of the book circles around. The idea is gathered in a verse in the second chapter, where Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And don't cling to doing nothing, either. That last part matters. The verse closes the easy exit. Letting go of the fruit is not the same as walking away from the field. Here Gandhi pushes against a misreading. Non-attachment, he wrote, does not mean not caring how things turn out. The one who lets go of the fruit is not careless. That person is wholly given to doing the task well, because nothing is being saved up for the reward. Attention that would have gone to the prize goes into the work itself. Gandhi had a picture for this elsewhere in his writing, in a little book called Hind Swaraj. The means, he said, are like a seed, and the end is like a tree. You can't plant one kind of seed and expect another kind of tree. So if you care about the end, care first about the means, because the means are the part actually in your hands. Put the two ideas side by side and the mango planter makes sense. She can't make the tree bear on her schedule. She can water it well tonight. Anasakti is that evening watering, done with full care, while the harvest is let go.
screen: `ANASAKTI: NOT CLINGING TO THE FRUIT.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK ALONE.` · `LETTING GO IS NOT NOT CARING.` · `THE MEANS ARE A SEED, THE END A TREE.` · then, large: `WATER IT WELL TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Pick one thing you're working on right now: a project, a conversation you're hoping goes well, a person you're trying to help. Notice how much of your mind is already standing at the finish line, waiting for the result. Gently walk it back to the part that's actually in your hands today. One small step. See yourself doing just that step, with care. On each out-breath, set the result down, the way you'd set down a bag you've been carrying. If you pray, you can offer the work, and its fruit, to Krishna, or to the one you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. He called it Anasakti Yoga: the work given fully, the fruit let go.
Your line: the tree watered anyway. Today, do one task as if no one will ever thank you for it, and do it well anyway. Water the tree. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Some who follow the Gita's path of action try to offer their daily work without clinging to its results, and some readers of Gandhi pair Gita 2:47 with his line that means and ends are like seed and tree.

match.prompt: the word on the cover — tap the pairs.

myth: for Gandhi, non-attachment means not caring how things turn out
he wrote the opposite: the one who lets go of the fruit gives full attention to doing the task well.
the Gita verse Gandhi leaned on also warns against clinging to doing nothing
your right is to the work alone, not its fruits; and don't cling to inaction either.
in Hind Swaraj, Gandhi says the end justifies whatever means it takes
he pictured the means as a seed and the end as a tree: what you plant decides what grows.

fork.setup: you're working hard for a good result you may never see. the work is slow and no one's watching. what does Gandhi's Gita ask of you?
options: stop, since the result is out of your hands.
do this step well, and let the result go.
work only on what pays off quickly.
fork.reveal: anasakti: your right is to the work alone, never its fruits, and not to doing nothing either. Gandhi said letting go of the fruit frees attention for the work itself.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: anasakti, non-attachment; the word Gandhi chose for the title of his Gita.

trapdoor: what you thought: non-attachment means not caring.
what it means: in Gandhi's Gita, it means giving the work full care while letting go of the fruit.
what a scholar hears: Gandhi's reading of the verse on the fruits of action sits close to his Hind Swaraj teaching that means and ends are seed and tree.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2:47 (the right to the work, not its fruits; no clinging to inaction)
Anasakti Yoga, Gandhi's introduction (renunciation of fruit as the Gita's central teaching; not indifference to the result)
Hind Swaraj, the chapter on brute force (means as seed, end as tree)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Gandhi's introduction to Anasakti Yoga calls renunciation of the fruits of action the Gita's central teaching, and says that renouncing the fruit does not mean indifference to the result but full absorption in the task.
Confirm the seed/tree image for means and ends is in Hind Swaraj (chapter on brute force) as paraphrased.
The mango-planting scene in the hook is invented for illustration and makes no factual claim.
Editor pass: the trapdoor no longer says Gandhi himself tied Gita 2:47 to the seed-and-tree image (that pairing is the script's, not a cited claim of his).

Audit: 'He found it gathered in a verse in the second chapter' attributed to Gandhi a specific link to 2:47 the introduction may not make; now 'The idea is gathered in a verse'. 'a common misreading' (unsourced) became 'a misreading'.
